## Introduction

These exercises cover the R and Quarto material from weeks 12 and 13:
R basics, data frames and data wrangling with _dplyr_,
data visualization with _ggplot2_, and Quarto documents.

::: callout-tip
#### Lecture page exercises
Make sure to do any of the exercises on the week 12 and 13 lecture pages that we did
not do in class, including those in the
[week 12 self-study section](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#self-study-vectors-and-data-types).
:::

## Setting up

1. Start an RStudio Server session at OSC and make sure your RStudio Project is open
   ([Working directory and RStudio Projects](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#working-directory-and-rstudio-projects)).
   You should already have a `week13` folder inside it from this week's lectures.

2. Create a new Quarto document and save it inside the `week13` folder as
   `w13_exercises.qmd`
   ([Creating a Quarto document](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document)).
   This will be your main document for these exercises.
   Add a YAML header with:
   - A title, your name as the author, and the date
   - Nested below `format:` and `html:`:
     `embed-resources: true` to make the document self-contained,
     `toc: true` for a table of contents, and `theme: cosmo`

   Render the document to check that the YAML header works.

3. Initialize a Git repository in your `week13` folder,
   either by opening VS Code and following the instructions from
   [week 5](../week05/w5b_git.qmd), or by using the Terminal tab in RStudio
   (next to the Console).
   Commit to the repo at least once before you push it to GitHub (see the last exercise).

::: callout-note
#### Notes
- Install any packages that you haven't installed yet in the console,
  _not_ in your Quarto document.
  Apart from installing packages, run all your code in code chunks.
- Add a header for each exercise (and each part of exercises) to your document,
  so it's easy to navigate the rendered document using the table of contents.
:::

## Exercise 1: R basics

1. Assign the value `5` to an object `week11`, and `10` to an object `week12`.
   Then, add the values of `week11` and `week12` and assign the result to a new object
   `total_weeks`, and print it.

2. Create a vector `v1` that contains the numbers 1 through 5,
   and check its data type.
   Then, change the value of the third element of `v1` to `"Midweek"`, and print `v1`.
   What is the data type of `v1` now, and why?
   What happens if you try to convert `v1` to a numeric vector?

3. Create a character vector `fav_food` with the names of five of your favorite foods.
   Replace the third element of the vector with a bird name,
   and extract the first and fifth elements.

## Exercise 2: Data frames and _dplyr_

1. Load the _tidyverse_ package, using a chunk option to hide the messages that are
   printed when you load it.
   Read the `metadata.tsv` file in the `garrigos/meta` folder in your personal dir,
   and save it as an object `metadata`.
   Recall that the working directory of your Quarto document is its folder, `week13`.
   How many variables and rows does `metadata` have?

2. In the `metadata` object, replace `dpi` with `_dpi` in the `time` variable,
   and `cathemerium` with `cath` in the `treatment` variable.

3. Look at the help for the `matrix()` function and create a matrix with the numbers
   1 to 10 in 2 rows and 5 columns, and assign it to a new object called `my_matrix`.

4. In week 12's first lecture, we worked with the `iris` data frame,
   which is one of the data sets that comes with R.
   For this exercise, we will use the `mtcars` data frame, which similarly comes with R.
   Start by storing `mtcars` in a new object called `my_cars`,
   then view the first 6 rows of `my_cars`.

5. Check the structure of the `my_cars` data frame,
   which shows the data types of the variables in the data frame.
   Compute the mean of the `mpg` variable of `my_cars`.

6. Select the columns `mpg`, `cyl`, and `hp` from `my_cars`, and display the first 6 rows.

7. Write a single "pipeline" that manipulates `my_cars` by:
   - Selecting columns `mpg` (miles per gallon) and `cyl` (number of cylinders)
   - Only keeping rows with `mpg` greater than 10 and `cyl` equal to 6
   - Renaming the `cyl` column to `cylinders`
   - Assigning the resulting data frame to an object called `my_cars_filtered`

8. Save the new data frame as a CSV file called `my_cars_filtered.csv` in your working directory.
   In the RStudio "Files" pane,
   check that the file is there and click on it to view it in the editor pane.

## Exercise 3: Data wrangling

For this exercise, instead of creating new objects, use pipes, unless explicitly stated.

1. List all the datasets available in the `ggplot2` package.
   Save the built-in dataset `midwest` as an object `midwest_datasets`,
   and use `midwest_datasets` to answer all the questions below.

2. Filter the rows with `poptotal > 30000` and `popdensity > 800`.

3. Select the first 11 variables of the dataset.
   Then, create a new column named `asian_ameri` by dividing `popasian` by `popamerindian`,
   and sort by `asian_ameri` in descending order.
   Save this output as a `new_dataset` object.

4. Compute the mean total population per state, naming the column with the mean `poptotal`.

## Exercise 4: Data visualization in a Quarto document

In class, we created a scatter plot, a box plot, and a bar graph.
For this exercise, you will create violin plots using the `midwest_datasets` object
--- read the _ggplot2_ documentation to see how to do that.

1. Create a violin plot with `state` on the x-axis and `area` on the y-axis.
   Facet the plot based on `category`.

2. Create a violin plot with `state` on the x-axis and `poptotal` on the y-axis.
   Add jittered points to the plot, and color only the points based on `category`.
   Is this point color a global or a local mapping? Explain.

3. In the previous plot, change the theme to `theme_bw()`,
   and fill the violins by `state` using manually chosen colors instead of the default colors.
   Save this plot as an object `violin_plot`, and print it.
   Using chunk options, add a figure caption, change the figure's width and height,
   and center-align it
   ([Figure options in Quarto documents](w13b_data-viz.qmd#figure-options-in-quarto-documents)).

4. Export `violin_plot` to a file `violin_plot.png` in your working directory.

5. Add a chunk option to one of the chunks with a plot
   so that the plot, but not the code, is shown in the rendered document.
   Also, write a sentence or two of Markdown text below each plot that describes what it shows.

6. Render your document.
   Then, download the HTML file
   (in the Files pane, check the box next to the file, then click `More` \> `Export`),
   open it on your computer, and check that it includes all your plots.

## Exercise 5: Publish your repo on GitHub

As before, publish your Git repo on GitHub.

1. Create a repository on GitHub, connect it to your local repo,
   and push your local repo to GitHub.

2. Create a new issue and tag GitHub users `@kstarr791` and `@jelmerp`,
   asking us to take a look at your work.

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>**1.** Objects and arithmetic</summary>

```{r}
week11 <- 5
week12 <- 10
total_weeks <- week11 + week12
total_weeks
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Type coercion</summary>

```{r}
v1 <- 1:5
typeof(v1)

v1[3] <- "Midweek"
v1
typeof(v1)
```

After replacing a number with a character string,
the entire vector has become a character vector,
because a vector can only contain one data type
([type coercion](../week12/w12a_r-basics.qmd#a-vector-can-only-contain-one-data-type)).

When you try to convert it back to numeric,
R will return `NA` (with a warning) for any elements that can't be converted to a number:

```{r}
as.numeric(v1)
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** A character vector</summary>

```{r}
fav_food <- c("pizza", "sushi", "tacos", "pho", "curry")
fav_food[3] <- "cardinal"
fav_food[c(1, 5)]
```

</details>

### Exercise 2

<details><summary>**1.** Read the metadata</summary>

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```
````

```{r, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
metadata <- read_tsv("../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
metadata <- read_tsv(here::here("assets/metadata.tsv"))
```

```{r}
metadata
```

`metadata` is a data frame (more specifically, a tibble)
with `r ncol(metadata)` variables and `r nrow(metadata)` rows.

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Replace parts of strings</summary>

```{r}
metadata |>
  mutate(
    time = sub(pattern = "dpi", replacement = "_dpi", x = time),
    treatment = sub(pattern = "cathemerium", replacement = "cath", x = treatment)
  )
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** A matrix</summary>

```{r}
my_matrix <- matrix(1:10, nrow = 2, ncol = 5)
my_matrix
```

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** The `mtcars` data frame</summary>

```{r}
my_cars <- mtcars
head(my_cars)
```

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Structure and mean</summary>

```{r}
str(my_cars)
mean(my_cars$mpg)
```

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Select columns</summary>

```{r}
my_cars |>
  select(mpg, cyl, hp) |>
  head()
```

</details>

<details><summary>**7.** A pipeline</summary>

```{r}
my_cars_filtered <- my_cars |>
  select(mpg, cyl) |>
  filter(mpg > 10, cyl == 6) |>
  rename(cylinders = cyl)
my_cars_filtered
```

</details>

<details><summary>**8.** Write a CSV file</summary>

```{r, eval=FALSE}
write_csv(my_cars_filtered, "my_cars_filtered.csv")
```

</details>

### Exercise 3

<details><summary>**1.** The `midwest` dataset</summary>

```{r, eval=FALSE}
data(package = "ggplot2")
```

```{r}
midwest_datasets <- midwest
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Filter rows</summary>

```{r}
midwest_datasets |>
  filter(poptotal > 30000, popdensity > 800)
```

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Select, mutate, and arrange</summary>

```{r}
new_dataset <- midwest_datasets |>
  select(1:11) |>
  mutate(asian_ameri = popasian / popamerindian) |>
  arrange(desc(asian_ameri))
new_dataset
```

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Mean population per state</summary>

```{r}
midwest_datasets |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(poptotal = mean(poptotal))
```

</details>

### Exercise 4

<details><summary>**1.** A faceted violin plot</summary>

```{r}
midwest_datasets |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = area)) +
  geom_violin() +
  facet_wrap(vars(category))
```

</details>

<details><summary>**2.** Violin plot with jittered points</summary>

```{r}
midwest_datasets |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = poptotal)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = category))
```

This is a local mapping:
because the color mapping is specified inside `geom_jitter()` rather than inside `ggplot()`,
it only applies to the points, and not to the violins.

</details>

<details><summary>**3.** Customized plot with figure options</summary>

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
#| fig-cap: "Total population per county in five Midwestern states"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
violin_plot <- midwest_datasets |>
  ggplot(aes(x = state, y = poptotal)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = state)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = category)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("gold", "skyblue", "salmon", "palegreen", "plum")) +
  theme_bw()

violin_plot
```

</details>

<details><summary>**4.** Export the plot</summary>

```{r, eval=FALSE}
ggsave(filename = "violin_plot.png", plot = violin_plot)
```

</details>

<details><summary>**5.** Hide the code of a chunk</summary>

Use the `echo: false` chunk option:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| echo: false
violin_plot
```
````

</details>

<details><summary>**6.** Check the self-contained document</summary>

Because you used `embed-resources: true` in the YAML header,
the plots are embedded in the HTML file itself.
Without that option, the plots would be stored in a separate folder,
and would not show up when you open only the downloaded HTML file.

</details>
